correctness.rationale: For six i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) trials with strictly positive stakes summing to one, a stake at least p already certifies probability at least p. In the complementary class p>1/6 is necessary and sufficient for feasibility, singletons lose and every set of size at least four wins. Up to and including 1/5 every pair wins; up to and including 1/4 beyond that, failed pairs intersect (at most five) and all triples win. In the final interval, all 15 perfect matchings meet the winning pairs and each pair is counted three times. Hence at least five pairs win. Failed triples are pairwise 2-intersecting, since otherwise their union plus at most one remaining singleton gives weight below 3p≤1. Such a family has size at most four: after choosing two triples with common pair, either all triples contain that pair or all are contained in the union of those two. The only five-winning-pair case is a star, since each matching then has exactly one winning pair; every triple wins in that case (a failed triple off the center, the remaining failed pair and the center would sum to less than 3p). Its probability exceeds the four-core baseline by p²(1−p)³(5p−1). Otherwise six winning pairs and sixteen winning triples already give that baseline exactly. Equal or nearly equal cores of sizes six, five and four realize the three laws with all six stakes positive. The strict light-stake inequality and the dominant equality example were checked separately, including the endpoints. This is a continuum proof, not a grid inference.
residual_risks: The optional rational-grid program does not exhaust real stakes; the extremal conclusions rely on the analytic proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Known broader regimes do cover individual ordinary cases but do not prove the light-stake continuum envelope; in particular their target p is strictly below the new light-stake bound. The conjecture is not a coverage theorem.

evidence: The five-weight proof includes attaining heavy-core profiles but its failed-pair/triple bounds use no more than five weights. The sixth positive stake adds new winning/losing subset constraints.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: An older bound p, even where known, gives no sharp strict excess. A five-stake minimizer gives a candidate for six stakes after perturbation, not the lower bound for every six-stake vector; the six-vertex matching and triple argument supplies that missing direction.

evidence: The mean-crossing/MMS formulations concern the ordinary unrestricted lower bound. Optimizing stakes at threshold t in 2002.06804v4 takes a supremum.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Same mean-crossing normalization is genuine overlap for the ordinary bound. Maximizing a fixed-threshold tail is not equivalent to minimizing it over light stakes (complementation would also change the event, probability and constraints).

originality.rationale: Supported for the sharp six-weight non-dominant envelope, hence the six-weight bound across the stated full interval, not for the general conjecture, its reciprocal-p cases or the binomial-tail formulas themselves. The closest five-weight result has two coincident envelope values on a strictly smaller feasible class. It does not bound the larger six-weight class from below. No verified source compared here supplies the full six-weight envelope.

value.rationale: Six is a meaningful finite case of the weighted mean-crossing question. Removing the immediate single-stake certificate isolates the genuinely collective tail mechanism. The three attained laws locate exact jumps caused by the strict light-stake constraint, and the last branch settles the competing matching/star and triple configurations. This supplies a sharp benchmark not determined by the unrestricted bound or a smaller-stake computation.
residual_risks: No result for more than six stakes or for unequal Bernoulli parameters is inferred.
